newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists argue on policy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists argue on policy.

text.p: French opposition Socialists and Communists argued on Monday over who would set policy if the left won France's parliamentary election despite opinion polls that show the ruling centre-right has re-built a clear lead.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, trying to divert attention from the polls and left-wing in-fighting, insisted the race was wide open. He said a centre-right win would be a "reward for lies" after what he called broken government promises.

Left-wing disarray is delighting the government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who portrays the Socialists as hostages to Communist dinosaurs unfit to solve problems starting with France's record unemployment of 12.8 percent.

Communist party boss Robert Hue said his small party, which wants big wage hikes for the low-paid and a referendum on a single European currency from 1999, should have a say in policy if the left wins the May 25-June 1 election.
"There will be no left-wing majority without all components of the left -- including the Communist party," Hue wrote in the daily, which has a hammer-and-sickle emblem on its front page.
"And, for this new majority to be formed, all components will have to decide the new policy together."

Jospin retorted that the party with the most votes should fix policy, especially on disputed issues such as Europe, and denied seeking hegemony over the left. The Socialists favour the common currency on conditions that stop short of a referendum.

"It's not the hegemony of one political group or another that decides, it's democracy," he said in Reims, northeastern France. "It seems logical to me that the guidelines that win the most votes on the first round should be applied," he said.

The two latest opinion polls showed the centre-right again regaining a lead after the race narrowed to neck-and-neck last week. French bonds and stock prices rallied on the news -- the CAC-40 stock index closed 2.25 percent higher.
The latest survey, for the daily Le Figaro, showed the ruling RPR-UDF coalition winning 338 to 370 of the 555 National Assembly seats in mainland France.
The Socialists and their allies were seen trailing on 162-185 with the Communists on 21-28. The far-right National Front was forecast to win up to three.
Political parties began airing television and radio spots on state-run channels as the campaign entered its final two weeks.

Juppe accused the left of lacking a clear programme for the economy. "It is extremely surprising that, on such important subjects (as the economy)...that our adversaries should be in such a state of flux," he told a news conference.

Shown by opinion polls to be deeply unpopular, Juppe said his "absolute priority" was to lower taxes and charges, continue welfare reforms and improve the climate for small businesses. He reiterated calls for the campaign to focus on issues rather than personalities.

Jospin hit out at the right over what he said were broken promises since President Jacques Chirac's appointed Juppe in 1995 promising a war on unemployment, which has since risen to 12.8 percent of the workforce from 11.7.
Re-electing the right "would be to reward lies", he told a news conference. "It would be continuation of today's failure."

Jospin, under pressure to spell out details of his policies such as how to create 350,000 private sector youth jobs, said that a Socialist-led government would enlarge a deal between unions and bosses letting older workers retire early.
Workers would be able to retire before the age of 60 if they had paid 40 years' social security contributions, and as long as young people were taken on in their place.
Both the Socialists and Communists accuse the government of planning a new bout of austerity to help France qualify for a single European currrency if the centre-right wins the election.
They disagree on many other issues apart from Europe.
Jospin wants to create 700,000 jobs, Hue 1.5 million.

Hue and Jospin agree on cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay, but Hue wants it done immediately. The Communists also want a raise of 1,000 francs ($175) a month for people earning less than 15,000 francs ($265) a month.
